(CNN) -- Massachusetts sued the U.S. government on Wednesday, challenging the constitutionality of a federal law that defines marriage as the union of a man and a woman. The state of Massachusetts says the Defense of Marriage Act denies same-sex couples essential rights. "We're taking this action today because, first, we believe that [the Defense of Marriage Act] directly interferes with Massachusetts' long-standing sovereign authority to define and regulate the marital status of its residents," Attorney General Martha Coakley said Wednesday afternoon. "Massachusetts has a single category of married persons, and we view all married persons equally and identically," she said. "DOMA divides that category into two distinct and unequal classes of marriage." The lawsuit argues that the act, which became law in 1996, denies same-sex couples essential rights and protections, including federal income tax credits, employment and retirement benefits, health insurance coverage and Social Security payments. "In enacting DOMA, Congress overstepped its authority, undermined states' efforts to recognize marriages between same-sex couples, and codified an animus towards gay and lesbian people," the state wrote in the lawsuit, which was filed Wednesday in federal court. Massachusetts, the first state to legalize gay marriage, said that about 16,000 same-sex couples have been married there since 2004, when it began issuing marriage licenses. Since that time, the lawsuit said, "the security and stability of families has been strengthened in important ways throughout the state. " The state is challenging Section 3 of the law, which defines marriage as "a legal union between one man and one woman as husband and wife" and a spouse as "a person of the opposite sex who is a husband or a wife." Before the act, the lawsuit argues, defining marital status was the prerogative of the states. The law "eviscerated more than 200 years of federal government deference to the states with respect to defining marriage," it said. The lawsuit also argues that the law forces Massachusetts to treat same-sex married couples differently from heterosexual married couples, particularly through determining who qualifies for the state's Medicaid program, known as MassHealth, and whether a same-sex spouse of a veteran can be buried in a veteran cemetery. "But for DOMA, married individuals in same-sex relationships in the commonwealth would receive the same status, obligations, responsibilities, rights, and protections as married individuals in different-sex relationships under local, state, and federal laws," the lawsuit said. The defendants named in the lawsuit include the Department of Health and Human Services, Secretary of Health and Human Services Kathleen Sebelius, the Department of Veterans Affairs, Veterans Affairs Secretary Eric Shinseki and the United States itself. Charles Miller, a spokesman for the Department of Justice, said the department will review the case but noted that President Obama supports the legislative repeal of the Defense of Marriage Act. In March, Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders -- the same Boston-based group that successfully argued in 2003 for same-sex marriage rights in Massachusetts -- also sued the federal government over Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act. Besides Massachusetts, three other states recognize same-sex marriages: Connecticut, Maine, and Iowa. Vermont and New Hampshire will join their company when same-sex marriages become legal later this year and early next year.

Attorney General Martha Coakley explained her office's motivation during a Wednesday press conference: "We're taking this action today because, first, we believe that [the Defense of Marriage Act] directly interferes with Massachusetts' long-standing sovereign authority to define and regulate the marital status of its residents." According to the legal complaint, this 1996 federal statute strips same-sex married couples of numerous crucial benefits and protections—ranging from federal tax credits to workplace and pension benefits, health coverage, and Social Security income.

The court filing states that Congress exceeded its constitutional bounds when passing DOMA, interfering with state-level recognition of same-sex unions while institutionalizing prejudice against gay and lesbian citizens.

As the pioneering state in legalizing same-sex marriage, Massachusetts has issued licenses to roughly 16,000 gay and lesbian couples since beginning the practice in 2004. The lawsuit notes that this policy has significantly bolstered family security and stability across the commonwealth during this period.

The legal challenge specifically targets Section 3 of DOMA, which restricts marriage definitions to unions between "one man and one woman as husband and wife," with spousal status limited to opposite-sex partners. The suit contends that regulating marriage was traditionally a state responsibility until this law essentially dismantled two centuries of federal deference to states on this matter.

Additionally, the complaint highlights how DOMA compels Massachusetts to treat gay married couples unequally compared to heterosexual married couples—affecting eligibility determinations for MassHealth, the state's Medicaid program, and whether surviving same-sex spouses of military veterans can be interred in veterans' cemeteries.

The lawsuit asserts that without DOMA's restrictions, same-sex married couples in Massachusetts would enjoy identical legal standing, benefits, and obligations as opposite-sex married couples under all levels of government law.

Named defendants in the case include the Department of Health and Human Services along with Secretary Kathleen Sebelius, the Department of Veterans Affairs and Secretary Eric Shinseki, and the federal government itself.

Justice Department spokesperson Charles Miller indicated that officials would examine the lawsuit's claims, while pointing out that President Obama favors repealing DOMA through congressional action rather than judicial intervention.

This isn't the first legal challenge to Section 3—back in March, the Boston-based organization Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders, which previously won the landmark 2003 case establishing same-sex marriage rights in Massachusetts, also brought suit against this same provision.

In a significant legal move, the Commonwealth of Massachusetts filed a lawsuit against the United States government, directly challenging the constitutionality of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA). This federal law, which defines marriage exclusively as a union between one man and one woman for federal purposes, has become the target of a state-level constitutional challenge that could have far-reaching implications for same-sex marriage rights across the country.

## Sovereignty and Equal Protection Concerns

At the heart of the lawsuit is Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley's argument that DOMA fundamentally interferes with the state's sovereign authority to define and regulate marital status within its own borders. Coakley contends that by imposing a federal definition of marriage that conflicts with state law, DOMA effectively creates two unequal classes of marriage—one recognized fully under state law, and another that remains second-class in the eyes of the federal government, regardless of its legal status at home.

## Denial of Essential Federal Benefits

The lawsuit further asserts that DOMA's practical effect is to deny same-sex couples access to a wide array of essential federal rights and benefits that opposite-sex married couples receive automatically. These include critical protections such as:

- Federal tax credits and deductions available to married couples
- Employment-related benefits and retirement plan protections
- Health insurance coverage extended through a spouse's employer
- Social Security payments and survivor benefits

By excluding same-sex couples from these federal programs, the state argues, DOMA imposes significant financial and practical hardships on families who are otherwise legally married under Massachusetts law.

## Congressional Overreach and Codified Discrimination

Massachusetts further argues that in enacting DOMA, Congress exceeded its constitutional authority. The lawsuit contends that the federal government has no legitimate basis for overriding individual states' determinations about who may marry, particularly when doing so undermines the validity of marriages that states have already deemed legal. According to the state's argument, DOMA does not merely decline to recognize same-sex marriages—it actively codifies discrimination against gay and lesbian individuals into federal law, treating them as unequal under a system that claims to guarantee equal protection to all citizens.

Central to the state's case is the real-world experience of Massachusetts since it became the first state in the nation to legalize same-sex marriage in 2004. **BOSTON** — Massachusetts Attorney General Martha Coakley has filed a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the federal Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), arguing the 1996 law unlawfully discriminates against same-sex couples who are legally married under state law.

The suit, filed in U.S. District Court in Massachusetts, contends that DOMA violates the Tenth Amendment by interfering with the state's authority to define and regulate marriage within its own borders. Massachusetts became the first state in the nation to legalize same-sex marriage in 2004.

"This law denies these families the same rights and protections that all other married couples receive at the federal level, based solely on the sex of the two people applying for marriage," Coakley said at a press conference announcing the litigation. "The federal government does not have the right to interfere with the way Massachusetts grants marriage licenses to its own citizens."

DOMA, signed into law by President Bill Clinton in 1996, prevents the federal government from recognizing same-sex marriages for the purposes of more than 1,000 federal statutes and programs, including tax filing status, Social Security survivor benefits, and health insurance coverage for spouses of federal employees.

Coakley's lawsuit argues that the law creates what she calls a "one-size-fits-all federal definition" of marriage that improperly overrides the authority states have historically held to set their own marital standards.

"For over 200 years, it has been the states, not the federal government, that has set the rules governing marriage," Coakley said. "DOMA disrupts that balance by requiring Massachusetts to discriminate against its own married citizens in order to receive federal funds."

The lawsuit specifically points to inequities faced by same-sex couples in Massachusetts who are legally married but denied access to federal marriage-based benefits afforded to opposite-sex couples. Coakley's office cited examples including surviving spouses unable to collect Social Security benefits and couples unable to file joint federal tax returns.

"These couples are married under Massachusetts law. They should not be treated as legal strangers by the federal government," Coakley added.

Legal experts say the case could set an important precedent, as it approaches the DOMA question from a states' rights angle rather than solely as a matter of individual civil rights, potentially appealing to a broader ideological coalition.

The Justice Department has not yet issued a formal response to the lawsuit. Under federal law, the department is typically obligated to defend existing statutes in court, though the Obama administration has faced internal and public pressure regarding its approach to DOMA-related litigation.

Reaction to the lawsuit has been divided along familiar lines. Advocates for same-sex marriage praised the move as a critical step toward full federal recognition of marriage equality, while opponents defended DOMA as a necessary measure to preserve a uniform federal definition of marriage.

Coakley said she expects the case to take months, if not years, to resolve, but expressed confidence in the state's legal position.

"We are simply asking the federal government to respect the laws of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts," she said. "Married is married."

The case is expected to be closely watched by legal scholars and advocacy groups on both sides of the marriage debate, as similar challenges to DOMA make their way through courts in other jurisdictions.

# Massachusetts Challenges Federal Marriage Law in Historic Lawsuit

In July 2009, Massachusetts became the first state to sue the federal government over the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA), marking a significant escalation in the legal battle over same-sex marriage rights. The lawsuit, filed by then-Attorney General Martha Coakley, argued that DOMA unconstitutionally interfered with the state's sovereign authority to define marriage and discriminated against legally married same-sex couples.

## Background: Massachusetts as a Marriage Equality Pioneer

Massachusetts earned its place at the forefront of the same-sex marriage debate in November 2003, when the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court issued its landmark ruling in *Goodridge v. Department of Public Health*. The 4-3 decision found that denying marriage licenses to same-sex couples violated the state constitution's guarantees of individual liberty and equality.

The ruling made Massachusetts the first state in the nation to legalize same-sex marriage, with couples beginning to wed in May 2004. In the years that followed, thousands of same-sex couples married in the Commonwealth, gaining state-recognized spousal rights including inheritance, medical decision-making authority, and parental rights.

However, a significant gap remained: while Massachusetts recognized these marriages, the federal government did not. This disconnect stemmed from the 1996 Defense of Marriage Act, signed by President Bill Clinton, which defined marriage for federal purposes as strictly between one man and one woman. This meant that even legally married same-sex couples in Massachusetts were denied over 1,000 federal benefits and protections tied to marital status—including Social Security survivor benefits, joint tax filing, and the ability to file joint bankruptcy petitions.

## The Legal Arguments

Massachusetts' lawsuit, *Massachusetts v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services*, took a notably different approach from other marriage equality litigation. Rather than primarily arguing that DOMA violated equal protection guarantees for same-sex couples (though this argument was present), the Commonwealth's central claim rested on federalism principles and states' rights.

The lawsuit contended that:

**1. Marriage Regulation is a State Matter**

Attorney General Coakley argued that domestic relations—including marriage—have traditionally been the exclusive province of state law. By creating a federal definition of marriage that overrode state determinations, DOMA exceeded Congress's constitutional authority and violated the Tenth Amendment, which reserves powers not delegated to the federal government to the states.

**2. Unequal Treatment of Married Couples**

The suit argued that DOMA forced Massachusetts to discriminate against its own legally married citizens in order to comply with federal law. For instance, the state couldn't provide certain federally-funded benefits, like Medicaid, equally to all married couples because federal law wouldn't recognize same-sex marriages, creating what the state characterized as an unconstitutional two-tiered marriage system.

**3. Spending Clause Violations**

Massachusetts also argued that DOMA improperly conditioned the state's receipt of federal funds (such as Medicaid funding for veterans' cemeteries) on the state's willingness to violate its own equal protection principles by treating married same-sex couples differently than married heterosexual couples for purposes of certain benefit programs.

## Political and Legal Context

The lawsuit emerged during a pivotal moment in the marriage equality movement. By 2009, several other states—including Connecticut, Iowa, Vermont, and New Hampshire—had also legalized same-sex marriage, but DOMA's federal restrictions affected couples in all of these jurisdictions equally.

The Obama administration, while stating opposition to DOMA as a policy matter, found itself in the awkward position of defending the law in court, as the Department of Justice traditionally defends existing federal statutes unless there's a compelling reason not to. This created tension with LGBTQ advocacy groups who had hoped for a more assertive stance from an administration that had voiced support for repealing DOMA.

Legal experts noted that the Massachusetts case was unusual in that it combined constitutional claims typically seen in individual civil rights cases with structural federalism arguments more commonly associated with conservative legal challenges to federal authority—creating an interesting cross-ideological legal strategy.

## Looking Ahead

While the Massachusetts lawsuit proceeded through the federal court system, it became part of a broader wave of legal challenges to DOMA nationwide. Similar cases, including *Gill v. Office of Personnel Management*, filed by GLAD (Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders) on behalf of individual same-sex couples, tackled the same federal statute from different angles.

These parallel legal challenges set the stage for what would become a defining constitutional battle over the following four years, ultimately contributing to significant developments in federal marriage law and same-sex couples' rights.

*This article reflects reporting on events as they unfolded in 2009. Subsequent legal developments, including Supreme Court rulings on DOMA and marriage equality, would further shape this evolving area of law in the years that followed.*

# Massachusetts v. U.S. Department of Health and Human Services: A Landmark Challenge to DOMA

## Background of the Case

In 2009, the Commonwealth of Massachusetts filed a significant legal challenge against the federal government, specifically targeting Section 3 of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA). This federal law, enacted in 1996, defined marriage for all federal purposes as a union exclusively between one man and one woman, effectively denying federal recognition to same-sex marriages even in states where such unions were legally performed.

## The Massachusetts Argument

Massachusetts, which had legalized same-sex marriage in 2004 following the state Supreme Judicial Court's decision in *Goodridge v. Department of Public Health*, built its case on several key constitutional arguments:

**Tenth Amendment Claims**: The Commonwealth argued that DOMA violated the Tenth Amendment by intruding on the state's traditional authority to regulate marriage. Massachusetts contended that marriage regulation has historically been a matter reserved to the states, and the federal government overstepped its constitutional bounds by creating a separate federal definition of marriage that conflicted with state law.

**Spending Clause Violations**: The state also argued that DOMA forced Massachusetts to discriminate against its own same-sex married couples in order to receive federal funding for certain programs, including Medicaid and veterans' cemeteries, creating an unconstitutional condition on federal funds.

**Equal Protection Concerns**: Massachusetts asserted that DOMA created two distinct classes of married couples within the state—those recognized by the federal government and those who were not—based solely on sexual orientation, violating principles of equal treatment under law.

## Legal Proceedings

The case proceeded through the federal court system, with U.S. District Judge Joseph Tauro presiding over the Massachusetts challenge (which was considered alongside a related case, *Gill v. Office of Personnel Management*, brought by GLAD - Gay & Lesbian Advocates & Defenders).

In July 2010, Judge Tauro issued a groundbreaking ruling, finding Section 3 of DOMA unconstitutional. He ruled that DOMA violated both the Tenth Amendment and the Spending Clause by forcing states to discriminate against their own citizens in order to receive federal funding, and by intruding on areas of traditional state authority.

## Broader Legal Context

This case emerged as part of a wave of legal challenges to DOMA occurring simultaneously across the country. It ran parallel to other significant cases, ultimately contributing to the legal momentum that led to the U.S. Supreme Court's landmark decision in *United States v. Windsor* (2013), which struck down Section 3 of DOMA as unconstitutional on equal protection grounds.

## Appeals Process

The federal government appealed Judge Tauro's ruling to the First Circuit Court of Appeals. In 2012, the First Circuit upheld the lower court's decision, finding DOMA unconstitutional, though it based its reasoning primarily on equal protection grounds rather than the Tenth Amendment arguments Massachusetts had emphasized.

## Significance

The Massachusetts case represented a unique approach among DOMA challenges, as it was brought by a state government asserting its sovereign interests rather than by individual same-sex couples asserting personal rights violations. This gave the case particular weight in constitutional federalism debates, adding a state's rights dimension to what might otherwise have been framed purely as a civil rights issue.

The case ultimately contributed to the broader legal landscape that resulted in nationwide marriage equality being established in *Obergefell v. Hodges* (2015).
